content: To achieve universal primary healthcare, it is essential to exercise political will, mobilize national resources, and use external resources judiciously. All nations must collaborate in a spirit of partnership and service, recognizing that the health of people in one country directly impacts and benefits others. The joint WHO/UNICEF report on primary healthcare provides a robust foundation for advancing and implementing primary healthcare globally. Achieving an acceptable level of health for all by the year 2000 was deemed possible through better utilization of global resources, much of which is currently allocated to armaments and military conflicts. A genuine policy of independence, peace, détente, and disarmament could redirect resources toward peaceful objectives, particularly accelerating social and economic development, with primary healthcare receiving its rightful share. The International Conference on Primary Healthcare calls for urgent and effective national and international actions to develop and implement primary healthcare worldwide, especially in developing countries, in alignment with technical cooperation and a New International Economic Order. Governments, WHO, UNICEF, international organizations, funding agencies, health workers, and the global community are urged to support commitments to primary healthcare by increasing technical and financial support, particularly in developing nations. Collaboration is essential to introduce, develop, and sustain primary healthcare in line with the principles of the Declaration of Alma-Ata. The Sixty-Second World Health Assembly reaffirmed the pivotal role of WHO in promoting primary healthcare globally and emphasized the need to strengthen health systems based on the Alma-Ata Declaration and the United Nations Millennium Declaration. It recognized the importance of integrating disease-specific programs with broader health system approaches to achieve health-related Millennium Development Goals. The Assembly also highlighted the need to learn from past experiences in primary healthcare and welcomed the 2008 World Health Report, which identified four key policy directions: addressing health inequities through universal coverage, centering care around people, integrating health into broader public policy, and providing inclusive leadership for health. This includes developing comprehensive health services, equitable and sustainable financing mechanisms, and integrating palliative care and symptom relief into primary healthcare. Governments were also encouraged to train and retain adequate health workers, integrate vertical programs into primary healthcare, improve access to essential medicines, and strengthen health information systems. The Director-General of WHO was requested to align the organization’s efforts with the Alma-Ata Declaration, support Member States in implementing primary healthcare, and facilitate the exchange of experiences and evidence-based practices. WHO was also tasked with fostering global coordination for health system strengthening and ensuring adequate funding for revitalizing primary healthcare. The Assembly adopted a framework for integrated, people-centered health services, emphasizing the inclusion of palliative care and symptom relief in primary healthcare. The importance of equitable access to controlled medicines for pain management and the need to address regulatory barriers were also emphasized. Recognizing the growing need for palliative care due to aging populations and the rise of chronic diseases, the Assembly highlighted the importance of integrating palliative care into health systems. It acknowledged the ethical responsibility of healthcare systems to alleviate suffering and emphasized the need for education and training in palliative care for healthcare providers. WHO was also tasked with collaborating with international organizations to promote the availability and balanced control of medicines for pain relief and palliative care.
